v.why: Lowering an excessively high learning rate stabilizes training and gives large accuracy gains (exps 73, 74, 72).
Raising an already high learning rate causes divergence and big drops (exps 67, 68).
With a tiny learning rate the net is undertrained in 243 epochs, so a larger step helps (exps 61, 62).
Reducing a very strong L2 penalty relieves underfitting (exps 11, 19).
Increasing an already strong L2 penalty further harms fit (exps 7, 8).
At small learning rates extra depth adds capacity without instability (exps 49, 46).
Strong regularization leaves a model that benefits from extra depth capacity (exps 45, 49).
Wider networks learn faster at small learning rates (exps 86, 89).
Removing depth at low learning rate reduces capacity and hurts accuracy (exps 59, 56).
With slow training, weaker weight decay lets the weights grow enough to fit (exps 11, 19).

raw:
I based these on the 100 experiments plus general knowledge of MLP training dynamics. The evidence is noisy, so these are best guesses.

- **Learning rate down at high LR.** Experiments 68, 73 and 74 show that lowering a too-high learning rate (0.02–0.08) gives large gains, and 72 shows a smaller one. Going up from a high LR (67, 68) hurts a lot.
- **Learning rate up at low LR.** Experiments 61 and 62 show gains from raising a very small LR, since the model is undertrained at 243 epochs.
- **Alpha down at high alpha.** Experiments 11, 19 and 8 show that reducing a strong L2 penalty helps. Experiment 11 gives +7, +9 and +15.
- **Alpha up at high alpha.** Experiments 7 and 8 show large drops from pushing the penalty higher.
- **Depth up at low LR.** Experiment 49 shows adding depth helps at LR 1e-5, with gains across all three datasets.
- **Width up at high width.** Experiment 89 and a few others suggest gains at low LR. For high-LR configs, width changes are risky, so I'm less sure here.
- **Batch size up at low LR.** Experiments 29 and 39 are mixed, so I treat this one as weak.
- **Depth up at high alpha.** Experiments 45 and 49 show gains with alpha 0.129 and 1, probably because more capacity offsets the regularization.
